title: Lights on the control panel
ask: Should the new control panel have its own lights showing what is on (defog, recirc, mode, each seat's heat or cool level), or should the cluster screen show them?
why: The new panel has nine keys and four knobs, and nothing on it lights up to show what is on. The seat knobs have no end stops: they turn forever and count clicks, so once you let go, nothing on the panel tells you whether the seat is on heat 2 or cool 1. The same goes for the defogger, recirculate and the HVAC mode. The factory panel had a lamp for the defogger. Your answer decides whether the panel gets its own lights. If it does, the ribbon to the DCU grows from 20 to 26 wires, a small LED driver goes on the panel, and the faceplate needs windows for the lights. If it doesn't, the ICU's screen shows the state instead.
options:
(a) Lights on the panel: an LED by each key and a short row of LEDs for each knob's level, run by a small LED chip on the panel over the DCU's existing I2C bus. The ribbon goes from 20-way to 26-way (+2 data wires, +5 V and spares). About $5-10 more in parts. The faceplate has to leave room for the lights.
(b) No lights on the panel: the ICU screen shows the climate, seat and defog state, as a strip on every page or a pop-up when a knob moves. No parts, and the ribbon stays 20-way. You have to look at the cluster to see a setting.
(c) One light only, for the defogger, as the factory had. This still needs one more conductor, so the ribbon goes to 26-way. The seat levels are shown on the ICU screen as in (b).
recommend: (a), unless you want the dash kept dark and are happy glancing at the cluster to see a setting
stops: The ribbon's size (P157), the panel board's layout (H-008) and the faceplate's drawing

title: What the control panel is built on
ask: Should the control panel's switches, knobs and diodes sit on a small ordered circuit board, or be hand-wired?
why: The panel has no computer, but its 9 key switches, 9 diodes, 4 knobs, the mirror stick and the ribbon socket still have to be mounted and wired together behind the faceplate. The wiring itself is settled (D-380, D-452). This decides what it is built on. A circuit board gets ordered alongside the DCU board, and the knobs and switches solder straight onto it. Hand wiring is free, but it means about 40 point-to-point wires behind the dash.
options:
(a) A small circuit board, ordered in the same order as the DCU board: about $10-20 more. The knobs and switches line up exactly with the faceplate, and it holds the lights if the panel gets its own lights. The faceplate has to be drawn first so that the board's holes match it.
(b) Hand-wired on perfboard or point-to-point: no extra cost, but more hours at the bench. The diodes become leaded parts instead of the tiny surface-mount ones. It is harder to line the knobs up with the faceplate holes, and harder to service.
recommend: (a), unless you would rather spend bench hours than about $15
stops: The panel's layout (H-008) and its parts list (P155)

title: How the pop-ups are driven
ask: Should each pop-up motor be driven the way Mazda does it, with a constant feed on WR and a changeover relay that sends power to either the UP (R) or the DOWN (RY) input, so the motor stops itself at the top and bottom?
why:
The 1982 factory diagram the research found (00-CAR SP-584) shows each motor has its own relay and cam switches inside. WR is the motor's power, R means "go up", RY means "go down", and the motor stops itself at each end. The current design caps WR and powers R and RY together as if they were the winding, so as drawn the lamps would not move, or would cycle until the 4-second trip.

It also feeds both relay coils (K1, K2) from O1, the output the windows share. So every window press would run both pop-ups.

CK08 (now a powered test) proves the motors match the diagram before anything is crimped.
options:
(a) Mazda's way: WR on the O1 bus, and K1/K2 used as changeovers (one per side) switching 12 V to R or RY. The windows can share O1 without moving the lamps, and the wink switches still work. One more conductor per side in the L2 leg; no new parts (K1/K2 are already changeover relays).
(b) Keep today's scheme by opening each motor and wiring around its internal relay and cam switches. The leg stays as drawn, but the motors lose their own end stops and rely on the 4 s timer. Undoing it means re-soldering the motors.
recommend: (a), unless CK08 shows the motors do not match the factory diagram
stops: The L2 leg pin plan (L2-P 3/4, L2-S 1/2), relays K1/K2, the A4/A5 transit sense, V-081 and the window bus (D-357)

title: What the fuel pump does when the oil sender reads open
ask: If the oil-pressure sender reads as an open circuit, should the PMU treat that as zero oil pressure and stop the fuel pump after the 3-second prime?
why:
The factory sender reads open circuit at 0 psi, and its resistance falls as pressure rises (00-CAR SP-787, 1985 manual). CK19 ohms the 1982 one.

The design treats an open reading as a broken wire and keeps the pump running, and its "above OIL_MIN" test points the wrong way. Together they mean the oil gate never stops the pump: after a stall, or a crash with the key on, it keeps pumping fuel.

An open sender and a broken sender wire look identical to the PMU, so one of the two cases has to lose.
options:
(a) Open = no pressure: the pump stops after the prime. A broken sender wire then stops the engine, and the cluster shows zero oil pressure, so you know why. Safest in a crash or a stall.
(b) Open = fault, keep pumping (today's intent, D-249). A broken wire never strands you, but the gate never works with this sender, because 0 psi reads open.
(c) A separate oil-pressure switch just for the pump gate: about $15-25 and one more conductor in L1. The gauge and the gate stop sharing a wire.
recommend: (a), unless you would rather spend about $20 on (c) so a sender-wire break can't stop the car
stops: Logic FUEL_PUMP, input A7, recovery RC07, and the swap's pump gate

title: What lights the dash at night
ask: Should the dome lamp go back to the factory way (always-hot feed, grounded by its own door switch) so O20 can light and dim the dash, cluster and radio with the headlight switch?
why:
O20 feeds both the dome lamp and the whole illumination bus: the dash lamps, the radio's illumination wire, the new panel, and the ICU's dimming reference. Its logic is "a door is open". So as drawn, the dash lights only with a door open, never with the headlights, and the ICU display runs at full daytime brightness at night.

The two can't share one output. If O20 followed the headlights, the dome lamp would glow whenever the lights are on. No PMU output is free.
options:
(a) The dome lamp goes back to the factory circuit (always-hot fuse, its own door switch), and O20 becomes illumination only: on with PARK/HEAD and dimmed by the dimmer. You lose the dome lamp's fade, and a door left open drains the battery, as it did from the factory.
(b) The dash illumination moves to the tail-lamp output O6 at full brightness (no dimming), and the dome lamp keeps O20 and its fade. The ICU and radio then know the lights are on but can't follow the dimmer.
recommend: (a), unless the dome lamp's fade matters more to you than a dimmable dash
stops: Pins O20/O6, node conductors N21/N22, logic INTERIOR, the ICU's dimming (DP-ICU-A 2), and the panel lighting (01.14)

title: Low-voltage shedding and the cluster
ask: Should the 11.5 V load shed leave the cluster (the ICU) on while the engine runs, and only act once the voltage has been low for about 10 seconds?
why:
Your D-248 rule sheds ACCESSORY, INTERIOR and COMFORT below 11.5 V, with no delay. ACCESSORY (O10) now powers the ICU and the speed sensor, and INTERIOR feeds its dimming.

Cranking sags to about 10.5 V, so the cluster would reboot on every start. A dying alternator would blank the speedo and the warnings exactly when you need them.
options:
(a) Shed only after about 10 s below 11.5 V, never during START, with about 0.5 V hysteresis, and keep O10 on while the engine runs. The ICU stays up; the comfort loads still shed.
(b) Keep D-248 as ruled and move the ICU's logic feed from O10 to IGNITION (O12). The cluster then ignores the shed, but it goes dark in ACC.
recommend: (a), unless you want the cluster dark in ACC anyway
stops: Rules voltage, logic ACCESSORY, and the ICU's power (DP-ICU-A 1)

title: Hazards and the 30-minute sleep
ask: Should the hazard lights keep the car awake for as long as they are switched on, even past the 30-minute forced sleep?
why:
The keep-alive rule turns the PMU off 30 s after the last change with the key out and the doors shut, and forces it off after 30 minutes regardless. It never looks at the hazard switch, so with the key out the hazards would stop after 30 seconds.

Adding the hazard switch to the 30 s rule is a plain fix. Whether the 30-minute limit also ends the hazards is your call (D-248).
options:
(a) The hazards keep the car awake with no limit. They flash until the pack's protection cuts in, many hours on the 40 Ah pack.
(b) The hazards keep it awake for up to 2 hours, then it sleeps to save the pack.
(c) The 30-minute limit wins: the hazards stop after 30 minutes.
recommend: (a), unless protecting the pack matters more to you than a stranded-car warning

title: Hatch and fuel-door release while driving
ask: Should the hatch and fuel-door releases only get power during the PMU's release pulse, even with the key on, so a stuck DCU output can never pop the hatch while driving?
why:
D-370 says the release relays have no power outside the pulse. That is only true with the key out: they are fed from an O10 tap, and O10 is on in ACC and RUN. With the key on, a panel press fires the solenoid at once, and one shorted transistor in the DCU would hold the hatch or fuel door open at speed.

The solenoid current is also unknown (the factory fuse is 20 A), so a release could trip O10, which now also runs the cluster. CK20 measures the solenoids.
options:
(a) Pulse-only feed: the release relays are powered through a small series relay that only the release pulse turns on, driven from O14 until the swap. One relay and socket, about $10. At the swap O14 goes to the fan, and the release needs another source then.
(b) Keep the O10 feed and add protection: a 10 A fuse of its own on the release branch (so a solenoid can't trip the cluster), pull-downs on the DCU's select transistors, and firmware that refuses a release unless the car is stopped and drops the select after 1.5 s.
recommend: (b), unless you want a hardware guarantee instead of a firmware one; then (a)
stops: Relays K3/K4, node conductor N85, logic ACCESSORY, SN23 and A11

title: Where the amplifier is fed
ask: Should the amplifier's power come off the load side of the master disconnect through its own fuse, so the disconnect really kills everything?
why:
D-236 feeds the amplifier straight off the battery posts. D-319 later put the master disconnect on the positive side so that one switch "genuinely kills the car". An amplifier on the post stays live with that switch open.

A fuse at a lithium pack also needs a high interrupt rating; that is why the main feed is a Class-T.
options:
(a) Off the disconnect's output stud, through its own MRBF fuse, sized once the amplifier class is chosen (block 03.13). The disconnect kills the amplifier too. About $30 for the fuse and holder.
(b) Keep it on the battery post (D-236), through a Class-T or MRBF. The amplifier stays live with the disconnect open, and you pull its fuse to work on it.
recommend: (a), unless you want the stereo to play with the car shut off at the disconnect

title: Three short feeds under the dash with no fuse of their own
ask: Should the three 10 AWG feeds from the busbar (to fuse block A, to the keep-alive relay K11, and from K11 to block B) each get a fuse at the busbar?
why:
Each is protected only by the 150 A main fuse. A chafed 10 AWG wire under the dash, with 150 A behind it, burns before that fuse opens.

The usual exemption is to keep each run under about 7 inches and sleeved. No row records that.
options:
(a) A fuse at the busbar on each, about 40 A: three holders, about $25.
(b) No fuses. Each run is kept under 7 in (180 mm) and double-sleeved, and that length is written into the rows and into E14.
recommend: (a), unless the node layout already puts the blocks right against the busbar
stops: Node conductors N03-N05, E14 and the parts list

title: Sizing the main feed for the swap
ask: Should today's backbone (2 AWG main feed, 150 A Class-T, the PMU) stay as it is, with the swap's big loads fed separately when the engine goes in?
why:
The swap plan (engine D-445) wants a 160 A alternator, with about 160 A of load when everything runs at once. Today every load goes through the PMU's stud and the 150 A Class-T on 2 AWG, and the alternator charges through a 100 A fuse on 6 AWG.

At 160 A the alternator fuse opens and the Class-T sits at its limit. Something has to change at the swap; the question is whether you pay for it now or then.
options:
(a) Keep today's backbone. At the swap, the radiator fan gets its own relay and fuse off the battery side, and the alternator gets a new 2 AWG-or-larger cable and a 200-250 A fuse. That work is in the engine bay, which is rebuilt anyway, so nothing bought now is wasted.
(b) Upsize now: a 1/0 main feed and a bigger Class-T, about $80-120 more. The PMU's stud still tops out near 170 A, so the fan has to come off the PMU either way.
recommend: (a), unless you want the backbone done once
stops: The engine's fan plan (LS_FAN, O14), F18/C07 at the swap, and engine D-445

title: Power for the seats
ask: Should the seats get their own fused feed straight from the busbar, sized for power-adjusted heated and ventilated seats, instead of sharing the 25 A comfort output?
why:
A14 is to be sized for "heat, ventilation and power-seat motors", but the comfort output O15 is 25 A, is shared with mirror heat and the servo rail, and is only on in RUN. Power-seat motors draw 10-20 A per seat. Many factory heated/cooled seats also carry their own module, grounded in the seat, instead of using the DCU's switched returns (D-382).

The seat pick (X-010) isn't made, and D-451 says the electrical build doesn't wait for it.
options:
(a) A separate fused feed to each seat from the busbar (about 30 A each, 12 AWG), switched by a relay, plus the DCU's heat/cool returns as today. It fits any seat; unused wire costs little. About $40.
(b) Manual seats only: heat and ventilation stay on O15 as D-382 has them, with no power-seat feed.
(c) Wait for the seat pick (X-010) before A14 is designed.
recommend: (a), unless you already know the seats will be manual

title: The DCU's comfort grounds
ask: Should the DCU's comfort connector use its spare cavity 8 as a third ground, so no ground pin carries more than its 13 A rating?
why: D-382 sends up to about 15 A through each of two size-16 ground pins, and those contacts are rated 13 A (series DT). Cavity 8 on the same connector is a spare with a sealing plug.
options:
(a) A third ground on DP-DCU-C 8: one more contact and a 14 AWG wire to the dash ground bus, about 10 A per pin.
(b) Keep two pins and lower the seat fuses so the worst case stays under 13 A per pin.
recommend: (a), unless you want to keep cavity 8 spare
stops: DP-DCU-C, G36 and the DCU carrier schematic

title: The window fuses
ask: What should the two window fuses (F8 driver side, F9 passenger side) be rated?
why: Both holders are in the design, but neither has a rating. The factory power-window circuit used one 30 A fuse for both doors (00-CAR SP-227). Each side now has its own holder on 14 AWG leads, good for up to about 20 A. The window motors aren't picked yet (LP36).
options:
(a) 20 A each: covers a stalled factory-type window motor, and the 14 AWG leads are fine.
(b) 15 A each: tighter protection, but a strong aftermarket motor may blow it at the end of travel.
recommend: (a), unless the chosen motor's stall current says otherwise

title: The DCU plug that mixes two harnesses
ask: Should all eleven DCU-B conductors come straight from the dash node as one tail, instead of eight arriving through the L3 leg at the post and three from the node?
why: DP-DCU-B cavities 1-8 (window commands and mirror lines) come through the L3 leg from the dash post. Cavities 9-11 (mirror heat and the release selects) are tails from the dash node. A plug fed by both means the L3 leg can't be unplugged at the post on its own, which breaks the rule that every leg unplugs (D-003).
options:
(a) One tail from the dash node: the eight conductors run from the node to the DCU directly, which frees eight cavities in L3-S2/L3-S3 at the post.
(b) Route 9-11 through the post in the L3 leg as well, using spare L3 cavities if there are enough.
recommend: (a), unless the node sits too far from the centre stack for a short tail
stops: DP-DCU-B, L3-S2, L3-S3, N84 and N86

title: Who makes the adapter for parts not picked yet
ask: For luxury parts that aren't picked yet (window motors, seats, radar, speakers, amplifier), should the electrical build end each run in a standard Deutsch plug and make a short adapter lead once each part is chosen?
why: D-450 says luxury is "put the parts in where the wiring is done", but factory and aftermarket parts come with their own connectors. A run can't end in the right connector for a part nobody has chosen. So either electrical does a little work after the freeze, or luxury crimps adapters, which D-450 says it never does.
options:
(a) Every run ends in a Deutsch plug. The adapter lead for each part is an electrical row gated on that part's pick: small work after the freeze, and the harness is never cut.
(b) Electrical waits for each pick and terminates in that part's own connector. No adapters, but the freeze waits on luxury's picks.
recommend: (a), unless you'd rather hold the freeze for the picks

title: Recovering the A/C refrigerant
ask: Should the A/C refrigerant be recovered by a shop before the interior strip, while the car can still be driven there?
why: B1 (strip the A/C) needs a shop to recover the refrigerant first. It is gated after the design freeze, which comes after the interior strip (S1), and by then the car can't be driven. That means a mobile service or a tow.
options:
(a) Drive it to a shop for recovery before S1: about $50-100 and an afternoon.
(b) Leave B1 where it is and use a mobile A/C service later: about $100-200.
recommend: (a), unless the system is already empty (worth a gauge check first)
